What a program was told, and what time it is.

The smallest thing that separates a program from a demo: until this existed,
nothing a Khora program did could depend on anything outside its own source.
Every path, every port, every setting was compiled in.

Two capabilities, and the split is the one `docs/design/permissions.md`
draws. `Env` is what the process was handed — its arguments and its
variables — and `Clock` is the time, which is a different kind of access and
a different thing to want to deny a dependency.

The C side is almost all ISO C: `getenv`, `strlen`, `memcpy`. There are two
exceptions, and both are things C has no portable answer for. The argument
vector is not returned by any C function, because it arrives through `main`
and is gone — so the generated `main` hands it to the runtime, and
`khora_arg` gives it back. And the clock is milliseconds, which is
`GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` on Windows and `clock_gettime` on Unix; ISO C's
`time` is whole seconds and there is nothing finer that is spelled the same
everywhere. The runtime already knows which target it was built for.

## Types

### EnvError

```khora
pub type EnvError = | Denied(name: String);
```

Why reading the environment did not work.

One case, because there is one way for it to fail that is not "no such
variable": the manifest did not grant it. Not being set is `None`, which is
an answer rather than a failure.

## Effects

### Env

```khora
pub effect Env {
  variable: (String) -> Option<String> raises EnvError,
  arguments: () -> List<String>,
}
```

What the process was started with.

A capability rather than plain functions, for the reason every other one is:
a function that reads `DATABASE_URL` says so in its signature, and a test
can hand it something else. Reading the environment is exactly the kind of
hidden input that makes a program hard to test, and this is the seam.

### Clock

```khora
pub effect Clock {
  unix_seconds: () -> Int,
  unix_millis: () -> Int,
  monotonic_millis: () -> Int,
}
```

What time it is.

Separate from `Env` because it is a different thing to deny: a library that
may read a configuration variable is not thereby a library that may know
how long something took, and a test that pins one usually wants to pin the
other differently.

**Two clocks, not one, and the split is not a detail.** A wall clock says
what time it is and can jump: NTP steps it, an administrator sets it, a
virtual machine resumes with a stale one — and it can jump *backwards*, so
subtracting two readings of it is not a duration, it is a guess. A monotonic
clock cannot go backwards and is what "how long did this take" actually
wants; its zero is arbitrary, so it can never be a timestamp.

One `millis` would therefore have been the wrong one about half the time,
and the half it was wrong for would be the half that only fails in
production, at 2am, when the clock is stepped an hour. Naming both makes the
caller say which they meant.

## Functions

### variable_or

```khora
pub fn variable_or(name: String, fallback: String) -> String with { env: Env } raises EnvError
```

A variable, or a default when it is not set.

The shape almost every caller wants, written once here rather than as a
`match` at each of them.

**The fallback is for "not set", not for "not allowed".** A denial passes
through rather than quietly becoming the default: a program told it may not
read `DATABASE_URL` and silently given `localhost` is a program that starts
and does the wrong thing, which is worse than one that stops and says why.
